claims.text: A microstructure-informed data-driven model can forecast Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness of HfNbTiVAl10.
Explicitly incorporating hierarchical heterostructural descriptors will improve predictive performance over conventional full-scale simulations.
The HfNbTiVAl10 alloy has a hierarchical heterostructure spanning multiple grain sizes, orientations, and phase distributions.
The proposed algorithm will use grain texture, phase-boundary, and dislocation-distribution features integrated from experimental and simulation datasets.
Predictions will be evaluated using standardized room-temperature uniaxial tensile and fracture tests at controlled strain rates.
Prior high-entropy-alloy studies have used controlled dynamic strain-rate conditions.
Variations in grain and sub-grain orientation mediate local mechanical response.
Dislocation accumulation zones and phase boundaries mediate local stress concentrations.
Hierarchical microstructural features govern fracture paths in HfNbTiVAl10.
Capturing multiscale interactions in the hierarchical heterostructure allows the model to avoid exhaustive atomistic simulations.
Microstructural details strongly influence mechanical properties in analogous high-entropy-alloy systems.
The proposed model will reduce computational prediction time by at least 50% relative to conventional simulation methods.
The proposed model will predict experimental mechanical properties within ±10% error.
Conventional simulations have prediction errors of ±15% or worse for the relevant tensile and fracture properties.
Full-scale molecular-dynamics and finite-element simulations are slower than the proposed model.
The model may lose validity when loading causes substantial microstructural evolution not represented in its training data.
High cyclic stresses or thermal fluctuations may produce out-of-distribution microstructural evolution that limits model performance.
The exact efficiency and accuracy improvements remain uncertain until the model is calibrated and validated specifically for HfNbTiVAl10.
Failure to achieve at least a 50% runtime reduction or consistent prediction errors exceeding ±10% will falsify the hypothesis.
